newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups, industry clash on U.S. mad cow proposal.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups, industry clash on U.S. mad cow proposal.

text.p: Consumer groups and and the cattle industry Thursday voiced clashing views over the Food and Drug Administration's proposal to ban the use of protein from cud-chewing animals such as cattle in feed for those animals.

In early January, the FDA proposed the ruminant feed ban to build a "firewall" against the spread of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, the so-called "mad cow disease." There have been no reported cases of BSE in the United States and FDA Commissioner David Kessler said the move would "build a protective barrier."
At a public forum led by a panel of FDA experts, consumer groups backed the proposed rule and suggested the FDA consider banning all mammalian protein from animal feed.

"This is the minimum protections that really would be acceptable," said Caroline Smith DeWaal, director of food safety at the Centre for Science in the Public Interest. "They really need to look at the issue of whether they need to go further than that."
"The risk here is of fatal brain disease. If they don't act before a case of BSE is discovered in this country I think this is going to come back to haunt them," she said.
But industry groups challenged the science behind the proposed rule and expressed concern about the environmental and economic costs.

"We do not believe it (BSE) can have an origin in the United States because all known research indicates the system is in place to protect against it," said Douglas Anderson, a member of the National Renderers Association.

Renderers are expected to be the most affected by the rule. FDA economists estimate it will cost renderers between $63.2 million to $252.8 million annualy in lost sales and $6.3 million annually to comply with the proposed rule.

The first case of mad cow disease was reported in Britain in 1986. Evidence gathered in the UK suggests an association between the outbreak of BSE there and the feeding to cattle of protein derived from sheep infected with scrapie. BSE and scrapie are transmissible degenerative neurological diseases.

Recently, scientists have linked BSE to a new variant form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, a fatal degenerative neurological disorder affecting humans. The disease, which leaves spongelike holes in the brain, has killed 10 people in Britain.
The FDA aims to release the final rule in mid-summer.
"I think there is a great deal of work to be done in order to achieve that," an FDA official said after the meeting.
